opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic logic is fairly straightforward if you take standard economic models seriously. If you expect AGI to arrive in the next decade or two, and you think it's going to dramatically accelerate economic growth, then you're expecting to be much richer in the future than you are today. And in most models of consumption smoothing, if you expect your future income to be much higher, you want to borrow against that future, or at least save less now, because an extra dollar of consumption today is worth a lot more to you than an extra dollar when you're already enormously wealthy.

You can see this through interest rates too. If people broadly came to believe that growth was going to jump from two percent a year to twenty or thirty percent, real interest rates would have to rise a lot. Nobody wants to lend money at three percent when they expect the economy, and their own consumption, to be ten times bigger in a decade. So one implication is that if markets really priced in transformative AI, you'd see much higher long-term real rates than we currently do. The fact that we don't is some evidence that markets aren't expecting it, or at least not with high confidence.

That said, I'd add some caveats. One is that the returns to capital might themselves be very high in an AGI world. If AI systems can substitute for labor, then owning capital, including compute and the firms that run these systems, could become extremely valuable, while labor income might stagnate or fall in relative terms. So for an individual whose main asset is their ability to work, the case for saving might actually get stronger, not weaker, because you want to hold claims on the part of the economy that's going to capture the gains. Whether you should save less depends a lot on whether you expect your own income to share in that growth.

There's also uncertainty. AGI might come later than people think, the transition might be bumpier, and there are scenarios where things go badly. Under that kind of uncertainty, keeping some buffer seems prudent. So I'd say expecting AGI does push in the direction of saving less, especially if you think broad prosperity follows, but the picture is more nuanced once you think about who captures the returns and how confident you really are in the timeline.

r001.rationale: It says that expecting much higher future income means wanting to borrow against that future or save less today.

r002.rationale: It explains that an extra dollar of consumption is worth more today than when someone is already enormously wealthy, conveying that marginal utility falls as future wealth rises.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the basic argument goes something like this. If you expect AGI within, say, the next ten or twenty years, and you expect it to lead to very rapid economic growth, then you expect to be much richer in the future than you are today. And the standard consumption-smoothing logic says that if you expect to be much richer later, you should consume more now and save less, because the marginal utility of a dollar to you today is a lot higher than the marginal utility of a dollar to a version of you that's a hundred times wealthier.

So on the surface, that argument seems pretty straightforward. But I think there are a few complications that make it less clear than people assume.

The first is that it depends a lot on what happens to returns on capital. If AGI leads to a world where capital becomes extremely productive, because you can turn capital into labor essentially by building more compute and running more AI systems, then the return on saving could go up enormously. And in that case, even if you expect to be richer in the future, the fact that each dollar you save today might compound into a very large amount could more than offset that. So it's not obvious that the income effect dominates the substitution effect here. It actually depends on your specific beliefs about how the transition plays out and what happens to interest rates.

The second complication is uncertainty. You might expect AGI with some probability, but you probably shouldn't be certain about it, and you shouldn't be certain about the timelines. If there's a meaningful chance that growth remains roughly like it is today for the next few decades, then saving still has a lot of value in those worlds. And because of the way marginal utility works, the worlds where you end up poorer are exactly the worlds that should get more weight in your decision. So some kind of hedging makes sense, which pulls back toward saving.

The third thing I'd say is that it matters a lot who captures the gains. If you expect a world with explosive growth but where the returns mostly go to owners of capital, then having a stake in that capital could be extremely important, and being someone who consumed everything beforehand could leave you in a relatively worse position. If instead you expect the gains to be broadly distributed through something like redistribution or very cheap goods and services, then the argument for saving less gets stronger, because your welfare won't depend much on what you personally own.

So my honest view is that the naive version of the argument, where you just say "AGI is coming, so spend your money now," is too simple. It smuggles in assumptions about interest rates, about certainty, and about distribution. When you actually work through the model, I think you can get either answer depending on those parameters. And personally, I lean toward thinking that if you genuinely believe in a high-growth AGI scenario, the case for holding assets that are exposed to that growth is actually quite strong, which is kind of the opposite of what people usually conclude.

r001.rationale: It says expected future wealth makes consumption-smoothing logic favor consuming more now and saving less.

r002.rationale: It explains that a dollar has higher marginal utility today than for a much wealthier future self, and that marginal utility also makes poorer outcomes matter more under uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I think the main argument is that if you expect AGI to lead to very rapid economic growth, you might expect to be much richer in the future. And one reason to save is to move consumption from a time when you're relatively well off to a time when you're relatively worse off. If the future is going to be much wealthier, that pushes toward consuming more today.

But there's a distinction between the world becoming richer and you becoming richer. If your income comes mostly from your labor, and AGI makes that labor less valuable, then you might actually want to accumulate assets before that happens. Owning some of the capital that benefits from AI could become more important.

There's also the question of returns. Faster growth could mean higher returns on investment, which makes saving more attractive, even if you expect future abundance. So I don't think expecting AGI straightforwardly implies that you should save less. It depends on how you expect the gains to be distributed, what assets you can own, and how confident you are about the timing. If there's substantial uncertainty, keeping a financial buffer still seems pretty valuable.

r001.rationale: It says expected future wealth makes saving less attractive because it favors consuming more today.

r002.rationale: It discusses consumption timing and possible income losses, but does not clearly identify a change in the marginal utility of income as a reason AGI expectations complicate saving less.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it pushes in that direction, but it’s not as straightforward as “AGI is coming, so you should spend all your money now.”

The basic argument is that if you expect to be much richer in the future, you should want to move some consumption into the present. If AGI produces a huge increase in economic growth and you expect to share in that prosperity, then saving to fund consumption decades from now becomes less attractive. You’re transferring resources from a relatively poor version of yourself to a relatively rich version.

But the important qualification is whether you actually expect to share in that wealth. Your wages might fall if AI can do your job, and it’s uncertain what redistribution will look like. In that world, owning assets could be particularly valuable. So expecting the economy to become much richer isn’t necessarily the same as expecting yourself to become much richer.

There’s also a distinction between saving for retirement and saving to have a buffer. Even if you think retirement saving is less important, having money available during a potentially disruptive transition could be more important.

So I think AGI weakens some conventional reasons for saving, especially if you’re confident that the benefits will be broadly shared. But uncertainty about the transition gives you a reason to retain some financial flexibility.

r001.rationale: It says that expecting to be much richer in the future makes saving for future consumption less attractive, shifting resources from a poorer present self to a richer future self.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about sharing in AGI-driven wealth, possible wage declines, and the value of a financial buffer, but does not identify a change in the marginal utility of income.
